newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces hold talks in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces hold talks in Afghanistan.

text.p: Forces opposed to Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia -- buoyed by a reversal in their waning fortunes -- met on Monday to discuss joint tactics as they fight their way back towards the capital Kabul.

Former Afghan government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood and northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum held talks in a trailer surrounded by snow-capped peaks at this strategic pass where the once-unstoppable Taleban have been turned back.
"Our forces have not yet entered the capital -- they are four km (2.5 miles) to the north," said Mohammed Daoud, secretary to Masood.
Earlier, the Taleban government conceded it had lost the northern frontline town of Jabal os-Siraj and was fighting ousted government forces around Bagram airbase, an hour's drive north of Kabul.
Taleban sources also said one of their senior commanders, Mullah Abdul Ahad, had been killed.
Daoud confirmed fighting was still going on round the airbase.
"Right now we don't have Bagram but we're going to take it soon," he told Reuters. "Masood holds some parts and the Taleban still have others."
The Taleban captured Kabul on September 27 and pushed north to bottle up Masood's forces in his Panjsher valley stronghold.
But Masood's battle-hardened guerrillas have pushed the Taleban most of the way back to the capital in the past two days.
General Said Jasser Naderi, a senior member of Dostum's forces, said so far Dostum's backing for Masood had been logistical.
"This meeting is to decide the future -- what we will do together," he told Reuters. "Working together is the only way to defend Afghanistan."
Asked if they planned to retake Kabul, he said: "We want to take it by negotiation if possible, but if that fails..."
The Taleban have taken power in about three-quarters of Afghanistan since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan.

But Masood, who won a reputation as one of the country's best guerrilla generals with his defences of the Panshjer valley against Soviet troops in the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist government, has them rattled now.

In addition to his push down the main road from the Salang, he has also orchestrated a series of hit-and-run attacks well behind the front lines, some of them as close as 15 km (nine miles) from Kabul.
